 Editorial: Uthmeier, Ingoglia are wrong for Florida in word and deed

 Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, left, and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia. (Orlando Sentinel photos) 
 By Orlando Sentinel Editorial Board | insight@orlandosentinel.com PUBLISHED: October 28, 2026 at 5:30 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... With a major election less than a week away, candidates and their consultants are pounding Floridians with a barrage of words — some intended to cast themselves in a flattering light, some intended to smear and degrade their opponents.
 At this point in the game, many candidates will say pretty much anything they think would win them votes. That’s why it’s time to take a step back. Don’t listen to the rhetoric. Consider the facts. And regardless of what political party (if any) you are registered to, and how you feel about the big issues of the day, there are some questions to which you — and most Floridians — should look for answers.
 What have candidates done to make you believe they are on your side? Have they spent their free time — or even their careers — fighting for people like you, or did they secure their power by scapegoating those who could not fight back? If they’ve held public office before, did they do a good job of keeping their promises — and were those promises made to benefit voters, or the wealthy interests that bankrolled their campaigns? Did they faithfully fulfill the duties of the offices they held? And how many times have they been caught lying to Floridians?
 In the races for two Cabinet-level posts, the answers are not pretty. Even before Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed James Uthmeier to the attorney general’s office and elevated Blaise Ingoglia to chief financial officer, both offered voters reasons for concern. Uthmeier was the dark architect of many of DeSantis’ most reprehensible schemes, including a plan that took money that the Legislature appropriated to be spent inside the state of Florida and blew it on flights that took asylum seekers from Texas to Martha’s Vineyard. He was also neck-deep in a scheme that took a $10 million settlement that should have gone to Medicaid and was instead diverted through the nonprofit Hope Florida and eventually to political campaigns. And the scant records around the outrageous boondoggle that poured more than $1 billion into a hellhole immigrant-detention camp in the Everglades point to him as the key engineer.
 Beyond that, during his term as attorney general, he’s made a habit of declaring laws he doesn’t like to be “unconstitutional” — including age limits on firearms purchases (which have been upheld across the nation) and sensible growth boundaries and a requirement to fairly draw legislative districts, both enacted by local voters. Uthmeier’s declarations are idiotic: Similar laws have passed constitutionality tests in other states and even here in Florida. Yet there’s no doubt that he values his own opinion above everyone else’s.
 Floridians have a better choice here. Jose Javier Rodriguez has worked hard to defend those who really need help — both as Assistant Secretary of Labor under Joe Biden and in the Florida Senate.
 As for Ingoglia, the best we can say is that his shenanigans haven’t been quite as blatant as Uthmeier’s. But the deception he’s practiced while wielding the authority of the CFO’s office might do more long-term damage. Soon after DeSantis appointed him to the CFO position, Ingoglia started barnstorming the state in an attempt to convince Floridians that government spending was out of control — not state spending (which was obviously going awry thanks to Uthmeier’s schemes) but at the county and city level. To make his point, Ingoglia launched phony audits of local governments, using a cockeyed formula that he claimed proved that spending was out of control and repeatedly using inaccurate numbers to back up his claims.
 If Ingoglia really wanted to point out wasteful spending, he should have done just that. We can only assume he couldn’t find many juicy examples — because local governments, for the most part, are held far more accountable for the money they budget, including a requirement to go to voters before taking on substantial debt.
 Unfortunately, his dog-and-phony show served a grimmer purpose. Florida lawmakers repeatedly cited his antics as the legitimate basis for proposed constitutional Amendment 3, which would eliminate non-school property taxes for homeowners. Earlier this week we offered solid reasons why voters shouldn’t vote for this boondoggle. The bottom line is this: This amendment is not really a tax cut but a massive tax shift, and one that could blow up in everyone’s faces — including the homeowners who supposedly would benefit. If it passes, Ingoglia will largely be to blame for building the foundation of lies that supported it.
 Florida voters have a worthy alternative here, as well. Annette Taddeo is a seasoned leader and small business owner who served in the Florida Senate, where she worked on legislation to defend the first responders that might be out of a job if Amendment 3 passes.
 When you take a look at both races, it should be clear: This is not a partisan issue. Republicans hate being lied to as much as Democrats do. Nonpartisan voters are just as disgusted by politicians who sacrifice the public good for their personal gain. And voters should be incensed when state officials take it upon themselves to ignore the will of the people, as expressed through local elections.
 Now Uthmeier and Ingoglia are standing before the same voters they repeatedly undermined and deceived, pretending to be accomplished incumbents. This should be an easy pick for Floridians, regardless of party.
 The Orlando Sentinel Editorial Board consists of Opinion Editor Krys Fluker, Executive Editor Roger Simmons and Viewpoints Editor Jay Reddick. Use insight@orlandosentinel.com to contact us.
